title: One login, one verifier
lesson: Keep each agent-host OAuth login tied to its own verifier: crossed transaction pairs fail PKCE.
limitations: Illustrative concurrent-login bug; not an observed product incident or the OAuth issuer mix-up attack.
A/B/C are symbolic; hash abbreviates the full S256 transform.
Token issuance assumes other OAuth checks pass; browser consent, redirects and permission enforcement are omitted.
Screen clearing is not revocation; the repair begins a fresh authorization attempt.
Audio analyzed but not physically listened to.

Original author evidence is retained separately; final encoded evidence and independent comparison are in reviews/comparisons/oauth-pkce/. No live provider test or continuous real-time playback review was performed.

transcript.text: The agent host starts login A, retains verifier A, and sends its S256 challenge. The server associates the returned code A with that challenge.
Login B starts alongside A with a different verifier and challenge. Both transactions have their own code and verifier.

An illustrative callback bug replaces the selected verifier in login A with verifier B. Code A and verifier B are sent together. The server derives a different challenge and rejects the exchange with invalid_grant; no token is returned.
The host abandons the confused local attempts and starts fresh login C with its own verifier and challenge. Clearing the diagram does not represent server-side revocation.
Code C and verifier C match the stored challenge. PKCE passes and, assuming the other OAuth checks pass too, the host receives a token. Tool permissions remain a separate check.

corrections: At 12.3s persist the wrongly selected verifier B in login A, with amber state and a brief shake, before the crossed pair is sent.
